LESSON 92 OF 106·Defensive Operations: Detect, Respond, Recover

The MITRE ATT&CK Framework for Defenders

ATT&CK as shared vocabulary: tactics, techniques, data sources and detections, and the honest limits of a knowledge base that describes what attackers do.

Applied Foundation16 min
Why this matters

ATT&CK is a shared vocabulary for what attackers actually do. For defenders its main value is coverage: it turns the vague goal of being secure into a checklist you can measure yourself against.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • A technique describes behaviour an adversary uses to reach an objective, and each has sub-techniques describing specific implementations.
  • Tactics are the reason for the technique, so the same technique may appear in different phases for different goals.
  • Software, industry and the adversary groups are published as separate matrices, which lets you compare your own relevance.
  • Mapping your detections to techniques makes coverage explicit and gaps arguable rather than invisible.
  • The framework is descriptive, not prescriptive: it tells you what is possible, not what is likely against you.

The background

  • It began as a way to document adversary behaviour from incident reports, because the knowledge existed only in people heads.
  • Organisations adopted it as a detection reference, and the detection and platform matrices followed.
  • Public incident reporting across sectors made the data set large enough to be genuinely representative.
  • It is now used for threat modelling and for procurement, as well as for detection coverage.

Real-world examples

  • A team with five hundred detection rules can still have no coverage of the techniques actually used against their sector.
  • Coverage measured by rule count is meaningless; coverage measured by technique is at least arguable.
  • Adversaries choose the technique that works against the defences in front of them, so they route around gaps.

What to look for

  • Check which techniques relevant to your sector you have visibility into, and start with the ones you lack entirely.
  • Check whether your detections produce usable context, since a technique alert with no detail is not actionable.
  • Check which sub-techniques you cover, because the specific implementation varies by group.
  • Check when your coverage was last reviewed, since it decays as systems change.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Read One Technique Page From Data Sources to Query

Walking a single technique from its data sources to a concrete query against a system you own, and testing whether the query survives a different implementation of the same technique

Open MITRE resource ↗

Key takeaways

  • Map your logging and detections to techniques, and treat unmapped techniques as the work list.
  • Start with the techniques most common against your sector rather than the most famous ones.
  • Use the framework to explain gaps to non-specialists, since the vocabulary is widely understood now.
  • Review coverage on a schedule, because a change in estate silently reduces it.
  • Use it for detection engineering and threat modelling, and ignore the parts you have no use for.
